To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
H5 HAs from currently circulating strains have a receptor-binding site (H5 RBS) that is more similar to human receptors than to avian receptors.

(i) the same RBS mutations in HAs from circulating strains do not lead to quantitative receptor switch, (ii) a single base pair change in the HA is sufficient to quantitatively shift receptor specificity, and (iii) the structural basis of the quantitative receptor switch in circulating HAs can be explained in terms of a single residue change at a position where the HAs are already divergent.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic determinants that govern the switch in receptor preference of H5 HA.
the molecular mechanisms of H5 HA adaptation and the identification of molecular markers that will allow us to monitor the emergence and transmission of H5N1 viruses.
the structural and functional determinants for the H5N1 HA to acquire a quantitative switch in binding from avian-like receptors to human-like receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a single base pair substitution in the RBS of H5N1 is sufficient to switch the binding preference of H5N2 from avian to the human receptor.
the mutations in the RBS of HA that lead to aerosols transmission in A/Vietnam and A/Indonesian viruses, do not quantitatively switch the receptor specificity in circulating H5NAs.
the H5N1 viruses that have been tested to date have a very low potential to transmit efficiently from person to person.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the H5N1 HAs from the currently circulating clades have a preadapted receptor-binding pocket and that the mutations identified in this study are required for H5N1 to quantitatively bind to human-like receptors.
the structural features of the RBS of the H5 HA are critical for the quantitative switch in receptor binding.
H5N1 viruses with the ability to transmit from person to person are likely to arise in the future, but that the emergence of such strains is unlikely to be a sudden event.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HAs from currently circulating clades are already primed for a switch in receptor specificity.
the H5N1 viruses currently circulating in poultry have the genetic potential to evolve the receptor-binding properties necessary to transmit efficiently among humans.
the HAs from circulating H5N2 and H5N8 viruses have already evolved the RBS features that are required to quantitatively shift their receptor specificity to human.
